title: Why not just buy the cheapest?
principle: Pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a Chennai company. In 1992, General Motors, the American carmaker, sold Sundram Fasteners its English factories making radiator caps, a small part that stops an engine boiling over. Sundram became GM's main cap supplier, and from 1996 to 2000, GM's Supplier of the Year.

screens.prompt: GM could buy caps from many firms. Why do you think it gave so much work to one?

options.label: Its caps were cheaper than other firms' caps
Its caps were good, year after year
GM had no other firm to buy from

screens.why: Good quality, year after year. A radiator cap costs little, but if it fails, the engine can overheat. Five Supplier of the Year awards in a row tell you Sundram kept earning GM's trust.

screens.title: Deming's point 4
screens.text: Here's the idea behind it. W. Edwards Deming, a famous American quality teacher, gave managers 14 rules. Rule 4: stop buying on the price tag alone. A cheap part can cost the most when it fails. Buy from as few suppliers as you can, for years, and help them improve.

screens.title: Now look at your bakery
screens.text: A carmaker and a home bakery both need parts they can trust. It's October, your fifth year. Each week you buy cream from whichever of five shops is cheapest. But the cream changes from week to week. Some weeks it won't whip, and cakes fail.

screens.prompt: The cheapest cream saves you ₹200 a week. But 2 cakes a week fail, and each costs ₹400 to bake again. Is it really cheaper?

options.label: Yes. It saves you ₹200 a week
No. It costs you ₹600 more a week

screens.why: Exactly. 2 failed cakes × ₹400 is ₹800 a week. Take away the ₹200 you saved, and the cheap cream costs you ₹600 more each week. That's Deming's point: the price tag isn't the whole cost.

wrong.a: That's the price tag. But 2 failed cakes × ₹400 = ₹800 a week. ₹800 minus the ₹200 you saved means you lose ₹600 a week.
wrong.b: Let's check. You save ₹200, but lose 2 × ₹400 = ₹800 on failed cakes. That's ₹600 a week worse, not even.

screens.prompt: Your sister says: buy from all five shops, so no shop can cheat you. Your cousin says: buy only from the best one. Who's right?

options.label: Your sister: buy from all five
Neither: buy from the best two
Your cousin: buy from the best one

screens.why: Right. Five shops means five kinds of cream. But only one can hurt too. In 1997, a fire hit the Aisin factory that made almost all of Toyota's brake valves, and Toyota's car plants in Japan stopped for days. So pick a few strong suppliers, not one.

wrong.a: Five shops means five kinds of cream, and none of them sees you as an important buyer. Two good shops still keep each other honest, and each one cares about your orders.
wrong.c: Close. Deming liked as few as possible. But in 1997, a fire at the Aisin factory, which made almost all of Toyota's brake valves, stopped Toyota's car plants in Japan for days. If your one shop stops, so do you. Keep a second good one.

screens.prompt: You now buy from two good shops. One shop's cream still fails about twice a month. What should you do first?

options.label: Show him a failed cake, and say what you need
Stop buying from him, and find a new shop
Pay him less for each bad week

screens.why: Exactly. Picking good suppliers is half of it. The other half is pushing them: show what went wrong, say what good cream means for you, like how thick and how fresh, and check it together. A supplier who knows your standard can meet it.

wrong.b: A new shop starts from zero, and may be worse. First show this one what went wrong, and tell him what good cream means for you. Push a good supplier before you drop one.
wrong.c: Paying less won't fix his cream. Show him the failed cakes, and agree on what good cream means, so he knows what to fix.

screens.prompt: Good suppliers tempt you with deals. Your butter shop offers 120 kg at once for ₹480 a kg, ₹20 off. You use 40 kg monthly. The catch?
screens.why: Exactly. 120 kg × ₹480 is ₹57,600, paid today, for butter you'll use over three months. You save ₹2,400, but for weeks most of that cash sits in your fridge. Remember frozen cash from Unit 1: cash in stock can't pay for Diwali.

wrong.a: You do save 120 × ₹20 = ₹2,400. But you pay 120 × ₹480 = ₹57,600 today, for butter you'll use over three months. That's frozen cash from Unit 1.
wrong.b: The butter is the same butter. The catch is the cash: 120 × ₹480 = ₹57,600 paid today, for butter that sits in your fridge for three months.

screens.setup: It's late October. Your best cream shop says it will close for five days at Diwali. That week you'll need 30 kg of cream for about 50 cakes. Your second good shop can't supply that much.
screens.question: How do you make sure you have good cream at Diwali?

options.label: Buy that week from the cheapest shops
options.outcome: The cheap cream won't whip on the busiest day of the year. 8 cakes fail: ₹3,200 to bake again, and four orders reach families late. Two of them complain in the colony WhatsApp group.
options.why: You were back to buying on price alone, on the week you could least afford a failed cake.
options.better: Test new shops before Diwali, and keep the best as a third supplier.

options.label: Test cream from three new shops now
options.outcome: You test cream from three shops on two cakes each, and one whips well every time. It covers the Diwali week. No cakes fail, and you keep it as your backup.
options.why: Exactly. You chose on quality, tested before you needed it, and now have a few strong suppliers, not one.

options.label: Ask your best shop to deliver extra early
options.outcome: The shop delivers a week's cream before it closes. By day four, some has gone sour. You throw away 6 kg and bake 2 cakes again. It works, just.
options.why: Getting it early saved the week, but fresh cream doesn't keep well, and you'll face the same problem every holiday.
options.better: Test new shops before Diwali, and keep the best as a third supplier.

screens.text: A shop buys rice from whoever is ___ each week, and the rice keeps changing. Deming would say: buy from a ___ strong suppliers.
screens.why: Exactly. Buying on price alone brings a different rice every week. A few strong suppliers, kept for years and pushed to improve, bring the same good rice every week.

summary: Deming's point 4: stop buying on the price tag alone. A cheap part can cost the most.
Work with a few strong suppliers for years, and push them to get better.
Keep a few, not one: if your only supplier stops, so do you.

cards.front: Cheap flour saves ₹150 a week, but 2 batches of bread fail at ₹300 each. Is it cheaper?
cards.back: 2 × ₹300 = ₹600 lost, minus ₹150 saved = ₹450 worse. Don't buy on price alone.

cards.front: How many suppliers for one key item?
cards.back: Few enough that each cares about you, more than one so a fire or a holiday can't stop you.

cards.front: A good supplier's goods fail now and then. What first?
options: Show them what failed, and agree a standard
cards.back: Pick good suppliers, then push them to get better.

sources.label: The bolts and nuts of enterprise (Madras Musings)
